name: Financial digitization
snapshot: I see more digital payments and financial services. I would look for networks that retain a share of volume after fraud and service costs. Fund movements show specific holdings; they do not prove why managers buy or sell. The United States and Europe are pushing faster payments and different rules. If volume grew without cash generation, I would examine where the value was going.
change: I am interested in how mobile devices, software and payment networks reduce the steps needed to move money. An intermediary’s opportunity depends on the fee it retains after incentives, fraud, funding and compliance.
arguments: Merchant acceptance and banking connections can create network effects and recurring use.
Account-to-account payments, competition and fee rules can reduce what an intermediary earns.
invalidation: If transactions increased but net revenue and cash per transaction deteriorated persistently, I would reassess the thesis. I would also examine who absorbs fraud losses.
value: I would examine networks whose acceptance, integration and scale are hard to replicate. A network’s power deserves attention, but it also invites regulation and alternatives. Its advantage interests me when it survives the cost of winning customers and providing the service.
evidence_text: I would keep observed results, surveys and announced targets separate.

name: Future consumption
snapshot: I see more digital shopping habits and consumers moving between channels. I would look for brands, distribution and logistics that sustain profitable repeat purchases. United States and European figures measure different things; I would read each with its denominator. Funds provide examples of exposure. I focus on whether advertising, returns or discounts consume the gains from growth.
change: Consumers move between stores, phones, platforms and subscriptions. I am interested in who brings them back without having to buy their attention again on every sale. Brand, service and the cost of reaching the customer matter here.
arguments: A recognized brand or an efficient distribution network can support repeat purchases and lower costs per order.
Advertising, discounts and returns can increase sales while making profitability worse.
invalidation: If repeat purchasing weakened and margins after advertising, logistics and returns fell persistently, I would reassess the thesis. Followers or visits would not compensate me for that loss.
value: I would examine brands with pricing power and platforms that bring together buyers, sellers and logistics. I would not call a popular brand a monopoly; I would ask for evidence of retention, margins and genuine difficulty in replacing it.
evidence_text: I would keep two panels: people shopping online in Europe and e-commerce’s share of United States sales. They measure habits and money; their denominators are different.

name: Water and food
snapshot: I see pressure on water, networks and agricultural productivity. I would look for measurement, treatment and equipment that save resources under collectible contracts. The United States and Europe provide specific programs and rules; capital movements need to be read through actual exposure. Scarcity supports the need, but tariffs, funding and the agricultural cycle can prevent the supplier from capturing value.
change: Usable water, food production and demand do not always coincide in the same place or at the same time. I am interested in investment that reduces leaks, improves treatment or produces with fewer inputs, and in who can pay for it.
arguments: Network maintenance and agricultural efficiency address physical needs that do not disappear with a fashion.
Public-sector customers can be slow to pay, and farmers can cut investment when their margins fall.
invalidation: If savings in water, energy or inputs did not justify the equipment’s cost, I would reassess the thesis. If a contract depended on an unviable tariff or subsidy, I would reassess its collectibility.
value: I would examine installed equipment requiring service, consumables and certification, as well as operators with clear concessions. A network can be a local monopoly; its returns remain tied to tariffs, mandatory investment and service quality.
evidence_text: I separate water stress, investment needs and efficiency outcomes. A country facing scarcity may need equipment while also struggling to finance it.

name: Space
snapshot: I see more space activity and services already embedded in communications and observation. I would look for contracts, spectrum and recurring customers. Funds and public procurement help me follow capital; regulation differs by country and mission type. I focus on whether launching and replenishing a constellation costs more than its users pay.
change: I am interested in the service coming from the satellite: connectivity, data, navigation or surveillance. Launch is one part of a chain that also needs ground stations, permits, maintenance and customers.
arguments: Orbital infrastructure can support recurring services and applications that are hard to provide from the ground.
Replacing satellites, insuring launches and competing for customers can consume substantial capital before revenue stabilizes.
invalidation: If utilization and renewals did not cover launch, replenishment and operation, I would reassess the thesis. More satellites in orbit would not solve that equation on their own.
value: I would examine authorized spectrum, operating networks, contracts and data that customers cannot easily replace. A strong launch position does not imply control of the entire space value chain or ensure that any listed company captures that value.
evidence_text: I separate satellites launched, service revenue and utilized capacity. Private operators’ share of launches is not a share of profits.

name: Critical materials
snapshot: I see concentrated mineral supply chains and efforts to diversify them. I would examine refining, separation and contracts before focusing only on the mine. The United States and Europe already have specific policies; public capital and funds leave different traces. I focus on whether substitution, oversupply or high costs could turn a strategic mineral into a poor investment.
change: Electronics, energy and defense need minerals processed to specific quality standards. I am interested in where the constraint lies: extraction, separation, refining or component manufacturing. Having the rock does not solve the whole chain.
arguments: Supply concentration and supply security can support investment in alternative capacity.
High prices attract supply and substitution. A new plant may need permanent support if its cost remains above competitors’ costs.
invalidation: If capacity grew faster than demand or prices failed to cover full costs over a meaningful cycle, I would reassess the thesis. I would also reassess it if the process failed to meet contracted quality.
value: I would examine refining processes, technical know-how and contracts that secure demand. A country’s concentration is not a company’s monopoly. For an alternative producer, I would care about its costs without assuming perpetual subsidies.
evidence_text: I read concentration by mineral and processing stage. A refining average does not let me assign the same dependence to copper, lithium and rare earths.

name: Education and the future of work
snapshot: I see a greater need to keep learning throughout working life. I would look for recognized credentials, employer integration and measurable outcomes. The United States and Europe provide different evidence and rules; listed exposure usually combines businesses. Funds show holdings, not educational quality. I focus on whether abundant, cheap content reduces pricing without improving employment or productivity.
change: Tasks change, and initial education can fall short. I am interested in who helps people acquire a useful skill and demonstrate it to an employer, with sustainable economics for both learner and provider.
arguments: Companies may need recurring training and credentials that lower the cost of assessing skills.
Free content and AI can make courses cheaper and make it difficult to charge for easily copied material.
invalidation: If learners did not achieve observable improvements and retention failed to cover the cost of attracting and training them, I would reassess the thesis. Enrollment counts are not enough for me.
value: I would examine assessment, accreditation and training integrated into work. The advantage may lie in recognition and employer relationships; a video library alone is less defensible.
evidence_text: I separate enrollment, skills and employment. More students or greater demand for an occupation does not prove to me that an educational platform will earn more.
